inline.s: Analyzing the atom, no form is ever produced;
Mind-only is what is established—the holders of evil views do not believe it.
It is no sphere for the sectarians, nor yet for the hearers;
What the Saviors of the world proclaim is the realm of self-realization.”

Then Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, for the sake of purifying the flow of what appears in the mind, asked the Buddha: “World-Honored One, how is the flow of what appears in the mind of all beings purified? Is it purified gradually, or is it purified at once?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, it is purified gradually, not at once. As the mango fruit ripens gradually, not at once, so do all the Tathāgatas purify the flow of what appears in the mind of all beings—gradually, not at once. As a potter shapes his vessels gradually, not at once, so do all the Tathāgatas purify the flow of what appears in the mind of all beings—gradually, not at once. As the great earth brings forth grasses and trees gradually, not at once, so do all the Tathāgatas purify the flow of what appears in the mind of all beings—gradually, not at once. Mahāmati, as a person learns music, writing, painting, and all the various arts gradually, not at once, so do all the Tathāgatas purify the flow of what appears in the mind of all beings—gradually, not at once. But as a bright mirror shows all images at once, without discrimination, so do all the Tathāgatas purify the flow of what appears in the mind of all beings—showing at once all realms free of marks, and yet without discrimination. As the sun and moon at one time illumine all forms and colors, so do all the Tathāgatas purify the past habits of the mind of all beings—at once revealing to them the inconceivable wisdom-realm of all the Tathāgatas. As the ālaya-consciousness at once reveals the body, the means of living, and the whole realm of the world, so too the Reward Buddha, in the Akaniṣṭha heaven, at once brings all beings to maturity and causes them to cultivate all practices. As the Dharma Buddha at once reveals the Reward Buddha and the Manifestation Buddha, and illumines with light the holy realm of self-realization, so too does he at once reveal the marks of the Dharma and illumine them, causing beings to depart from all evil views of being and non-being.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, as for what flows from the nature of the Dharma: the Buddha teaches the self-marks and common marks of all dharmas, the causal marks of the habit-energy of what appears in the mind, and the causal marks grasped by the imagined nature; mutually bound together, all these phantasms have no self-nature of their own, yet beings grasp them with every kind of attachment and take them as real—all of which can never be obtained.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, attachment to the imagined nature arises depending on the dependent nature. Mahāmati, as a magician, by the power of his illusion, conjures various forms of beings out of grasses, trees, tiles, and stones, and those who see them make all sorts of discriminations, none of them real—so too is this. Mahāmati, by the power of the habit-energy of grasping at realms, within the dependent nature the various marks of the imagined nature appear; this is called the arising of the imagined nature. Mahāmati, this is called the marks of the Dharma as taught by the Buddha who flows from the nature of the Dharma.

“Mahāmati, the Dharma Buddha establishes the sphere of self-realized wisdom, beyond the self-nature and marks of the mind. Mahāmati, the Manifestation Buddha teaches giving, morality, patience, effort, meditative concentration, and wisdom, the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, and all the liberations and the modes of activity of the consciousnesses; he establishes distinctions, transcends the views of the sectarians, and goes beyond the formless practices. Moreover, Mahāmati, the Dharma Buddha is not what can be encountered by clinging; all that is clung to, all the marks of what is made, and the marks of the measure of the faculties—all these he is utterly free of. He is not the realm grasped by ordinary people, by the two vehicles, or by the sectarians who cling to the mark of a self. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should diligently cultivate the marks of the holy realm of self-realized wisdom, and swiftly abandon the marks of the discriminations that appear in your own mind.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, the vehicle of the hearers has two kinds of distinguishing marks: the mark of the holy wisdom of self-realization, and the mark of clinging to the imagined nature. What is the mark of the holy wisdom of self-realization? It is this: clearly seeing the realms of the truths of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and no-self, and so, free of desire and quiescent, one knows as it truly is that the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, whether one's own or shared, are marks that do not perish; the mind abides in a single object, and abiding in a single object it attains the fruits of the way of dhyāna, liberation, and samādhi, and so is released. Abiding in the bliss of the realm of self-realized holy wisdom, it has not yet left behind habit-energy and the inconceivable death by transformation—this is called the mark of the realm of self-realized holy wisdom of the vehicle of the hearers. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, though he too attains this holy wisdom, out of compassion for beings and upheld by his original vows, does not realize the gate of quiescence and the bliss of samādhi; the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should not cultivate this bliss of self-realized holy wisdom. Mahāmati, what is the mark of clinging to the imagined nature? It is this: knowing such dharmas as hardness, moisture, warmth, and motion, blue, yellow, red, and white—that they arise not from a maker, yet relying on teaching and reasoning, one sees the self-marks and common marks and clings to them with discrimination—this is called the mark of clinging of the vehicle of the hearers. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should know and should abandon this dharma; departing from the view of the selflessness of persons, he enters the mark of the selflessness of dharmas and gradually abides in the grounds.”

Then Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, the first-principle realm of self-realized holy wisdom, permanent and inconceivable, which the Tathāgata has spoken of—is it not the same as the permanent and inconceivable maker spoken of by the sectarians?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, it is not that the maker of the sectarians attains the permanent and inconceivable. Why is this? The cause of the sectarians' permanent and inconceivable is that its own mark is not established. Since the cause's own mark is not established, by what is the permanent and inconceivable shown? Mahāmati, if the permanent and inconceivable spoken of by the sectarians had its own mark established as a cause, then it would be permanent; but because they take a maker as the causal mark, the permanent and inconceivable is not established. Mahāmati, my first-principle permanent and inconceivable is established by the causal mark of the first principle; it is far from being and non-being, and because it is the mark of the sphere of self-realized holy wisdom, it has a mark; because the wisdom of the first principle is its cause, it has a cause; because it is free of being and non-being, it is not a maker; because it is the quiescent dharma of space and nirvāṇa, it is permanent and inconceivable. Therefore I speak of the permanent and inconceivable, unlike all the disputations of the sectarians. Mahāmati, this permanent and inconceivable is the truth of the sphere of self-realized holy wisdom of all the Tathāgatas; therefore the Bodhisattva should diligently cultivate it.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, the sectarians' permanent and inconceivable is permanent because of the causal mark of an impermanent and differing mark, not because of the power of its own mark as cause. Mahāmati, the sectarians' permanent and inconceivable: seeing that produced dharmas, having existed, again become nonexistent, they infer from that impermanence that it is permanent. I too see that produced dharmas, having existed, again become nonexistent, yet on account of that impermanence I do not declare it to be permanent. Mahāmati, the sectarians establish the permanent and inconceivable by such a causal mark; this causal mark is nonexistent, the same as a hare's horn, and so their permanent and inconceivable is mere discrimination, nothing but words. Why is their cause the same as a hare's horn? Because it has no self-cause mark. Mahāmati, my permanent and inconceivable takes self-realization as its causal mark, and does not take external dharmas, which having existed again become nonexistent, and their impermanence, as its cause. The sectarians are the opposite of this: they can never know the mark of the self-cause of the permanent and inconceivable, and they forever remain outside the mark of the sphere of self-realized holy wisdom—this should not be spoken of.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, the hearers, fearing the suffering of the vain imaginings of birth and death, seek nirvāṇa, not knowing that the marks of the difference between birth and death and nirvāṇa are all only vain discrimination and are nothing whatsoever. They vainly imagine that the future cessation of the faculties and their objects is nirvāṇa, not knowing that realizing the realm of self-wisdom and turning the ālaya-consciousness, the support, is the great nirvāṇa. Those foolish ones speak of three vehicles, and do not speak of mind-only, in which no realm exists. Mahāmati, those people do not know the realm of the mind spoken of by the Buddhas of past, future, and present; grasping at realms outside the mind, they turn unceasingly in birth and death.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, the Tathāgatas of past, future, and present speak of all dharmas as unborn. Why? Because what is seen by the mind has no nature, and because it is free of the arising of being and non-being. Like the horns of a hare or a horse, which the foolish vainly grasp, it is only the sphere of self-realized holy wisdom, not the realm of the twofold discrimination of the foolish. Mahāmati, the body, the means of living, and the vessel-world, all are images of the ālaya-consciousness, appearing as the two marks of the grasped and the grasping; those foolish ones, fallen into the two views of arising, abiding, and ceasing, vainly give rise within them to discriminations of being and non-being. Mahāmati, you should diligently cultivate this meaning.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, there are five kinds of lineage. What are the five? They are: the lineage of the hearers, the lineage of the solitary realizers, the lineage of the Tathāgatas, the indefinite lineage, and the lineage without nature. Mahāmati, how does one know it is the lineage of the hearers? When one hears the self-marks and common marks of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields spoken of, and whether one understands or realizes them, the hair of the whole body stands on end and the mind delights in cultivating them, while one takes no delight in observing the marks of dependent arising—one should know this to be the lineage of the hearers. Having seen what is realized in his own vehicle, he cuts off the knots of affliction at the fifth and sixth grounds, but does not cut off the habit-energy of affliction, and dwells in the inconceivable death. He roars the lion's roar: ‘Birth is exhausted for me, the holy life is established, what was to be done is done, I shall receive no further existence.’ He cultivates the selflessness of persons, and even gives rise to the notion that he has attained nirvāṇa. Mahāmati, there are also beings who seek to realize nirvāṇa, saying that to be able to know and perceive a self, a person, a being, a nurturer, a grasper—this is nirvāṇa; and others say that to see all dharmas as existing through a maker is nirvāṇa. Mahāmati, they have no liberation, because they have not yet seen the selflessness of dharmas. This is the lineage of the hearers and of the sectarians; in what is not liberation they give rise to the thought of liberation—one should diligently cultivate and abandon this evil view.

“Mahāmati, how does one know it is the lineage of the solitary realizers? When one hears the dharma of the vehicle of the solitary realizers, the hair of the whole body stands on end, one weeps and sheds tears, and one is free of the entanglements of commotion and clings to nothing. Sometimes, hearing it said that they manifest various bodies, now gathered and now scattered, with supernormal transformations, one's mind believes and accepts without opposition—one should know this to be the lineage of the solitary realizers, and one should teach them the dharma of the vehicle of the solitary realizers.

“Mahāmati, the dharmas realized by the lineage of the Tathāgatas are of three kinds: the dharma of nature and no-nature, the dharma of the holy wisdom of inner self-realization, and the vast dharma of the realms of the external Buddhas. Mahāmati, if, hearing each of these dharmas and the inconceivable realm of the ālaya-consciousness set up by the body, wealth, and what appears in one's own mind, one is neither astonished, nor terrified, nor afraid, one should know this to be the nature of the lineage of the Tathāgatas.

“Mahāmati, as for the indefinite lineage: when one hears these three dharmas, one gives rise accordingly to faith and understanding and cultivates in accord with them. Mahāmati, the lineage is taught for the sake of those newly treading the ground, wishing to cause them to enter the ground free of images—this is the establishment made. Mahāmati, those hearers who abide in the bliss of samādhi, if they can realize and know the consciousness that is their own support, and see the selflessness of dharmas and purify the habit-energy of affliction, will in the end attain the body of the Tathāgata.”
“The stream-winner and the once-returner, the non-returner and the arhat;
All these holy ones—their minds are wholly bewildered.
The three vehicles I establish, the one vehicle and no vehicle;
Are taught for the foolish of scant wisdom and the holy ones who delight in quiescence.
The gate of the first principle is far from the two graspings;
Abiding where no realm is, how can three vehicles be set up?
The dhyānas and the immeasurables, the formless samādhis;
And even the cessation of feeling and perception—mind-only is not to be obtained.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, why is it that the icchantika gives rise to no delight in liberation? Mahāmati, because he has abandoned all roots of goodness, and because he has made vows for the sake of beginningless beings. How has he abandoned all roots of goodness? He slanders the bodhisattva collection, saying: ‘This is not a teaching that accords with the scriptures, with discipline, and with liberation.’ When he speaks these words, his roots of goodness are wholly cut off and he does not enter nirvāṇa. How does he make vows for the sake of beginningless beings? The Bodhisattvas, by the skillful means of their original vows, vow that all beings shall enter nirvāṇa, and ‘if even one being has not entered nirvāṇa, I shall never enter.’ He too dwells in the path of the icchantika—this is the mark of the lineage without nirvāṇa.”
Mahāmati the Bodhisattva said: “World-Honored One, who is it here that never enters nirvāṇa?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva-icchantika knows that all dharmas are nirvāṇa from the very beginning, and so never enters it; he has not abandoned the roots of goodness. Why? The icchantika who has abandoned the roots of goodness may, by the Buddha's majestic power, at some time bring forth roots of goodness. Why is this? Because the Buddha never abandons any being. Therefore the Bodhisattva-icchantika does not enter nirvāṇa.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should well know the marks of the three self-natures. What are the three? They are the imagined nature, the dependent nature, and the perfected nature. Mahāmati, the imagined nature arises from marks. How does it arise from marks? Depending on the dependent nature, the various kinds of marks of things appear, and one gives rise to attachment to them. Mahāmati, that attachment to the marks of things gives rise to two kinds of imagined nature, which the Tathāgatas have proclaimed: the attachment to the marks of names, and the attachment to the marks of things. Mahāmati, attachment to the marks of things is attachment to inner and outer dharmas; attachment to the marks of names is attachment to the self-marks and common marks within those inner and outer dharmas—these are called the two kinds of marks of the imagined nature. Mahāmati, what arises from what is depended upon and what is clung to is the dependent nature. What is the perfected nature? It is the suchness of the sphere of self-realized holy wisdom, free of all discrimination of the marks of names and the marks of things. Mahāmati, this is the perfected nature, the mind of the tathāgatagarbha.”
“The marks of names and their discrimination, the marks of the two self-natures; right wisdom and suchness—
These are the perfected nature.

“Mahāmati, this is called the gate of the dharma of observing the marks of the five dharmas and the self-natures, the sphere of self-realized holy wisdom; you and all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should diligently cultivate it.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should well observe the two marks of selflessness. What are the two? They are the mark of the selflessness of persons and the mark of the selflessness of dharmas. Mahāmati, what is the mark of the selflessness of persons? The aggregates, elements, and sense-fields are free of self and what belongs to self; produced by unknowing, craving, and karma, the eye and the other consciousnesses arise and grasp at forms and the rest, giving rise to attachment. Moreover, the body and the vessel-world seen by one's own mind are all manifested by the storehouse mind, changing and perishing unceasingly in a continuity of instants, like a river, like a seed, like the flame of a lamp, like a swift wind, like a floating cloud; restless and unsettled as a monkey, delighting in unclean places as a fly, never knowing satiety as a raging fire; with beginningless false habit-energy as their cause, they turn without rest through all the realms of existence like a water-wheel; the various bodily forms and their dignified deportments, advancing and halting, are like a corpse that moves by the power of a spell, or like a wooden man set in motion by a mechanism. If one can well know these marks, this is called the wisdom of the selflessness of persons.

“Mahāmati, what is the wisdom of the selflessness of dharmas? It is to know that the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields are of the imagined nature; that, as the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields are free of self and what belongs to self, they are only bound together by the rope of craving and karma, mutually arising in dependence, with no one who makes them; that the aggregates and the rest are likewise free of self-marks and common marks, and that the various marks appear as false discrimination, discriminated by the foolish but not by the holy ones. Observing all dharmas in this way, free of mind, manas, and consciousness, and of the five dharmas and the self-natures—this is called the wisdom of the selflessness of dharmas of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Having attained this wisdom, he knows there is no realm; comprehending the marks of the grounds, he at once enters the first ground, and his mind gives rise to joy; advancing by stages, he reaches the Ground of Excellent Wisdom and the Dharma Cloud, and all that was to be done is done. Abiding on that ground, there is a great jewel lotus king adorned with a multitude of jewels; upon that flower is a jewel palace shaped like a lotus, brought to accomplishment by the Bodhisattva's cultivation of the gate of the dharma of the nature of illusion, and he seats himself upon it, surrounded before and behind by his fellow Buddha-sons. All the Tathāgatas in all the Buddha-realms extend their hands and consecrate his head, as a wheel-turning king's son is consecrated. He transcends the ground of the Buddha-sons, attains the self-realized dharma, and accomplishes the Tathāgata's sovereign Dharma-body. Mahāmati, this is called seeing the mark of the selflessness of dharmas; you and all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should diligently cultivate it.”

Then Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, I pray you teach the marks of establishment and slander, so that I and all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas may depart from this evil view and swiftly attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi; and having attained bodhi, may refute the eternalist establishment and the annihilationist slander, and cause no one to slander the true Dharma.”
The Buddha accepted his request and spoke these verses:
“Body, possessions, and dwelling-place—all are images of mind-only.
The foolish cannot understand this, and give rise to establishment and slander;
What arises is only mind; apart from mind, nothing is to be obtained.”

Then the World-Honored One, wishing to speak this meaning again, told Mahāmati: “There are four kinds of the establishment of what does not exist. What are the four? They are: the establishment of a mark where there is no mark, the establishment of a view where there is no view, the establishment of a cause where there is no cause, and the establishment of a nature where there is no nature—these are the four. Mahāmati, as for the slanderer: he seeks and cannot find what the evil views have established, and failing to observe well, he gives rise to slander—this is the mark of establishment and slander. Mahāmati, what is the establishment of a mark where there is no mark? It is to give rise to attachment toward the self-marks and common marks of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, which are from the first nonexistent, thinking ‘this is so and not otherwise’; and this discrimination arises from beginningless evil habits—this is called the establishment of a mark where there is no mark. What is the establishment of a view where there is no view? It is to establish views of self, person, and being regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields—this is called the establishment of a view where there is no view. What is the establishment of a cause where there is no cause? It is this: before the first consciousness, nothing arises without a cause; the first consciousness itself is nonexistent, and afterward eye, form, light, and attention arise as causes producing it as an illusion; having arisen it exists, and having existed it again ceases—this is called the establishment of a cause where there is no cause. What is the establishment of a nature where there is no nature? It is to cling to and establish the nature of the uncompounded, beyond number and cessation, of space and nirvāṇa. Mahāmati, this is free of nature and no-nature; all dharmas are free of being and non-being, like a hair-net, like the horns of a hare or a horse—this is called the establishment of a nature where there is no nature. Mahāmati, establishment and slander are both the discrimination of the foolish, who do not understand mind-only; they are not the way of the holy ones. Therefore you should diligently observe and depart from this view.

“Mahāmati, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva well knows mind, manas, and consciousness, the five dharmas, the self-natures, and the marks of the two selflessnesses, then for the sake of beings he manifests various bodies, as the imagined nature arises depending on the dependent, and as a maṇi jewel shows colors according to the mind. He enters everywhere into the assemblies of the Buddhas and hears the Buddhas teach that all dharmas are like an illusion, like a dream, like a shadow, like an image in a mirror, like the moon in water; he is far from arising and ceasing, from annihilation and eternity, and does not abide in the way of the hearers or the pratyekabuddhas. Having heard, he accomplishes immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of samādhis; having attained these samādhis, he journeys throughout all the Buddha-lands, makes offerings to the Buddhas, is born in the heavens, glorifies the Three Jewels, manifests Buddha-bodies, and for the assemblies of hearers and Bodhisattvas teaches that all external realms are only mind, causing them all to depart from the attachments of being and non-being and the rest.”
“The Buddha-son can observe and see that the world is only mind.
He manifests various bodies, and all his actions are unobstructed;
With the sovereign power of supernormal penetration, he accomplishes all things.”

Then Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again requested the Buddha: “I pray you teach me the marks of the emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and non-self-nature of all dharmas. When I and all the Bodhisattvas awaken to these marks, we shall depart from the discriminations of being and non-being and swiftly attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

The Buddha said: “Listen well, and I shall teach you. Mahāmati, emptiness is the very meaning of the imagined nature. Mahāmati, it is because of clinging to the imagined nature that emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and non-self-nature are taught. Mahāmati, in brief, there are seven kinds of the nature of emptiness: the emptiness of marks, the emptiness of self-nature, the emptiness of no-action, the emptiness of action, the emptiness of the inexpressibility of all dharmas, the great emptiness of the holy wisdom of the first principle, and the emptiness of each and every one. What is the emptiness of marks? It is that the self-marks and common marks of all dharmas are empty, because they are mutually dependent, heaped up and awaiting one another; because, analyzed and sought out, they are nothing whatsoever; and because self, other, and both are all unborn; the self-marks and common marks are unborn and also un-abiding—therefore it is called the emptiness of the self-marks of all dharmas. What is the emptiness of self-nature? It is that the self-nature of all dharmas is unborn—this is called the emptiness of self-nature. What is the emptiness of no-action? It is that the aggregates are nirvāṇa from the very beginning, with no actions whatsoever—this is called the emptiness of no-action. What is the emptiness of action? It is that the aggregates arise from the conjunction of karma and causes, free of self and what belongs to self—this is called the emptiness of action. What is the emptiness of the inexpressibility of all dharmas? It is that the imagined nature of all dharmas is beyond words—this is called the emptiness of the inexpressible. What is the great emptiness of the holy wisdom of the first principle? It is that, when one attains self-realized holy wisdom, all views and habitual faults are utterly abandoned—this is called the great emptiness of the holy wisdom of the first principle. What is the emptiness of each and every one? It is that here there is no that—this is called the emptiness of each and every one. For example, in the hall of Mrgara-mata there are no elephants, horses, oxen, or sheep, and I say that hall is empty, but not that the assembly of bhikṣus is absent. Mahāmati, it is not that the hall lacks the self-nature of a hall, nor that the bhikṣus lack the self-nature of bhikṣus, nor that other places lack elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep. Mahāmati, the self-marks and common marks of all dharmas, sought one by one, are unobtainable; therefore it is called the emptiness of each and every one. These are the seven kinds of emptiness. Mahāmati, this emptiness of each and every one is the crudest of emptinesses; you should keep far from it.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, as for non-arising: the self-substance does not arise, and yet it is not non-arising; except for those abiding in samādhi, this is called non-arising. Mahāmati, as for non-self-nature: it is spoken with a hidden meaning because of non-arising. Mahāmati, all dharmas have no self-nature, because they do not abide for even an instant and because they are seen to change afterward—this is called non-self-nature. What is the mark of non-duality? Mahāmati, light and shadow, long and short, black and white, are all established in mutual dependence, and alone they are not established. Mahāmati, nirvāṇa is not outside birth and death, nor is birth and death outside nirvāṇa; birth and death and nirvāṇa have no marks of contradiction. As with birth and death and nirvāṇa, so it is with all dharmas—this is called the mark of non-duality. Mahāmati, the marks of emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and non-self-nature—you should diligently study them.”
“I always teach the dharma of emptiness, far from annihilation and eternity;
Birth and death are like an illusion, a dream, and yet karma is not destroyed.
Space and nirvāṇa, and the extinction of the two—so too is this;
The foolish vainly discriminate, while the holy ones are free of being and non-being.”

Then the World-Honored One again told Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: “Mahāmati, this emptiness, non-arising, non-self-nature, and mark of non-duality are all contained in the sūtras spoken by all the Buddhas; the scriptures spoken by the Buddha all have this meaning. Mahāmati, the various sūtras are spoken in accord with the minds of all beings, and the truth is not really in the words. For example, a mirage deceives and confuses the beasts, causing them to give rise to the thought of water where in truth there is no water; what the many scriptures teach is likewise so. They accord with the foolish, each according to his own discrimination, and cause him to give rise to delight, but they do not all reveal the true dharma of the holy wisdom's realization. Mahāmati, you should accord with the meaning and not cling to the words.”

Then Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, it is said in the sūtras that the tathāgatagarbha is pure in its intrinsic nature, permanent and unchanging, without alteration, endowed with the thirty-two marks, and present within the body of every being, wrapped in the soiled garment of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, and defiled by the stains of the false discriminations of greed, hatred, and delusion, like a priceless treasure within a soiled garment. The sectarians say that the self is a permanent maker, free of the guṇas, sovereign, and undying. Is the meaning of the tathāgatagarbha as spoken by the World-Honored One not the same as the self spoken of by the sectarians?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, the tathāgatagarbha I teach is not the same as the self spoken of by the sectarians. Mahāmati, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Fully Awakened One, teaches the tathāgatagarbha by way of such expressions as emptiness of nature, the ultimate, nirvāṇa, non-arising, markless, and wishless, in order to cause the foolish to depart from the fear of selflessness; he teaches the gate of the tathāgatagarbha, the realm free of discrimination and images. The Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas of future and present should not cling to it as a self. Mahāmati, as a potter, out of a lump of clay, by human effort, water, stick, wheel, and cord, makes various vessels by his skillful means; so too the Tathāgata, within the dharma of selflessness that is free of all marks of discrimination, by various kinds of wisdom, skillful means, and cleverness, speaks sometimes of the tathāgatagarbha and sometimes of selflessness, with various names, each one different. Mahāmati, I teach the tathāgatagarbha in order to gather in the sectarians who cling to a self, to cause them to depart from false views and enter the three liberations, and swiftly to realize anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. Therefore the Buddhas teach the tathāgatagarbha, which is not the same as the self spoken of by the sectarians. If one wishes to depart from the views of the sectarians, one should know the meaning of the selflessness of the tathāgatagarbha.”
Then the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The person, the continuity, the aggregates, the many conditions, and the atom;
The sovereign lord and maker—these are but discrimination of the mind.”

Then Mahāmati the Bodhisattva, surveying all the beings of the future, again requested the Buddha: “I pray you teach me the dharma of perfect cultivation, by which the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas accomplish the great cultivation.”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is complete in four dharmas accomplishes the great cultivation. What are the four? They are: observing what appears in one's own mind; departing from the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing; well knowing the no-nature of external dharmas; and single-mindedly seeking self-realized holy wisdom. If the Bodhisattvas accomplish these four dharmas, they are then called great cultivators. Mahāmati, what is observing what appears in one's own mind? It is to observe that the three realms are only one's own mind, free of self and what belongs to self, without action, without coming or going, perfumed by beginningless habit-energy of attachment, and manifested by the discriminations that follow and enter into the bondage of the body and its support, with the various colors, actions, and names of the three realms. Thus does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva observe what appears in his own mind. Mahāmati, how does one depart from the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing? It is to observe that all dharmas arise like an illusion, like a dream; because self, other, and both are all unborn; because they appear according to the measure of one's own mind; because external things are seen to be nonexistent; because the consciousnesses are seen not to arise; and because the many conditions are not accumulated, and discrimination causes the three realms to arise from causes and conditions. When one observes in this way, all dharmas, whether inner or outer, are unobtainable; knowing that they have no substance and are far from the view of arising, one realizes the nature of illusion, and at that very moment attains the unoriginated dharma-patience, abides on the eighth ground, comprehends mind, manas, and consciousness, the five dharmas, the self-natures, and the realm of the two selflessnesses, turns the support, and obtains the mind-born body.”
Mahāmati said: “World-Honored One, for what reason is it called the mind-born body?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, the mind-born body is so called because it goes like a thought, swift and unobstructed. Mahāmati, as the mind, beyond a hundred thousand yojanas, remembers the various things it has formerly seen, and thought following thought swiftly reaches there, and its own body, mountains, rivers, rocks, and walls cannot obstruct it—so too is the mind-born body. Adorned with the marks of the sovereign power of the illusion-like samādhi, remembering its original vow to bring beings to maturity, it is born among all the holy assemblies as a thought goes forth; this is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva's attainment of freedom from the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing. Mahāmati, what is observing the no-nature of external dharmas? It is to observe all dharmas as a mirage, as a dream, as a hair-net; because beginningless idle talk and all manner of clinging and false evil habits are their cause. When one observes all dharmas thus, this is the single-minded seeking of self-realized holy wisdom. Mahāmati, this is called the Bodhisattva's accomplishment of the great cultivation by being complete in four dharmas; you should diligently cultivate it thus.”

Then Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again requested the Buddha: “I pray you teach the marks of cause and condition of all dharmas, so that I and all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas may comprehend their meaning, depart from the views of being and non-being, and not vainly cling to the gradual or sudden arising of dharmas.”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, dharmas produced by cause and condition are of two kinds: inner and outer. The outer is this: by the conditions of a lump of clay, water, a stick, a wheel, a cord, and human effort, a jar is brought into being; as with the clay jar, so too with thread and woven cloth, grass mats, sprouts, curds, and butter—this is called the outer turning of cause and condition, arising one after another. The inner is this: unknowing, craving, karma, and the rest produce the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields—this is the inner dependent arising, which the foolish alone discriminate.

“Mahāmati, there are six kinds of cause: the cause of becoming, the cause of connection, the cause of marks, the efficient cause, the manifesting cause, and the cause of dependence. Mahāmati, the cause of becoming is when inner and outer dharmas act as cause and produce a fruit. The cause of connection is when inner and outer dharmas act as condition and produce the fruit of the aggregates and seeds. The cause of marks is when it makes an uninterrupted mark and produces a continuous fruit. The efficient cause is when it acts as the predominant condition and produces a fruit, like a wheel-turning king. The manifesting cause is when discrimination arises and can manifest the marks of a realm, like a lamp illumining things. The cause of dependence is when, at the time of cessation, the continuity is cut off and no vain imagining arises. Mahāmati, this is the foolish's own discrimination; it is neither gradual arising nor sudden arising. Why? Mahāmati, if it were sudden arising, then the maker and what is made would have no difference, and the causal mark would be unobtainable. If it were gradual arising, the mark of its substance would likewise be unobtainable—as when a son is not yet born, how can one be called a father? Those who calculate say that dharmas produced by cause, by the condition of the object, by the immediate condition, and by the predominant condition, the produced and the producer mutually bound and arising in sequence, are established by reasoning—but this cannot stand, for they are all marks of the clinging of false emotion. Mahāmati, the gradual and the sudden are both unborn; there is only what appears in the mind as body and possessions, and because the outer self-marks and common marks have no nature, only the arising of the consciousnesses and one's own discriminating views remain. Mahāmati, therefore one should depart from the views of gradual and sudden arising within the marks of the conjunction of cause, condition, and action.”
“All dharmas are unborn, and likewise there is no ceasing.
Within those very conditions, one discriminates marks of arising and ceasing;
It is not that the meeting of conditions is denied, that thus it ceases and arises again.
It is only to stop the foolish, who cling with false emotion;
Whether dharmas exist or not within conditions, they are wholly unborn.
Habit-energy confuses and turns the mind; from this the three realms appear;
From the first there is no arising, and likewise no ceasing.
Observe all that is compounded as a flower in the sky;
Free of the grasped and the grasping, and of all deluded views.
There is no producer and no produced, and likewise no cause or condition;
Only in accord with worldly custom does one speak of arising and ceasing.”

inline.s: Then Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, I pray you teach me the gate of the dharma of the mind regarding the marks of verbal discrimination, so that I and all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, well knowing this, may comprehend the two meanings of the speaker and the spoken, swiftly attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, and cause all beings to become purified in these two meanings.”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, there are four kinds of the marks of verbal discrimination: the verbal expression of marks, the verbal expression of dreams, the verbal expression of the clinging to past faults, and the verbal expression of beginningless vain imagining. Mahāmati, the verbal expression of marks is the arising of clinging to the marks of forms of one's own discrimination. The verbal expression of dreams is the recollection, upon waking, of realms formerly experienced in a dream, arising dependent on an unreal realm. The verbal expression of the clinging to past faults is that which arises from remembering former deeds of enmity. The verbal expression of beginningless vain imagining arises from the habit-energy of beginningless idle talk and vain clinging. These are the four.”
Mahāmati again said: “World-Honored One, I pray you further teach the marks of the sphere of verbal discrimination. Where, from what cause, and how does it arise?”
The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, it arises from the conjunction of the head, chest, throat, and nose, the lips, palate, teeth, and tongue.”
Mahāmati again said: “World-Honored One, is verbal discrimination different from it, or not different?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, it is neither different nor not different. Why? Because discrimination is the cause that gives rise to speech. If it were different, discrimination should not be the cause; if it were not different, speech should not make the meaning manifest. Therefore it is neither different nor not different.”
Mahāmati again said: “World-Honored One, is it speech that is the first principle, or is it what is spoken?”

The Buddha told Mahāmati: “It is neither speech nor what is spoken. Why? The first principle is the realm of the holy ones' delight, entered by means of speech, but it is not speech itself. The first principle is the realm of inner self-realization of holy wisdom; it is not the realm of the wisdom of verbal discrimination, and verbal discrimination cannot reveal it. Mahāmati, speech arises from arising, ceasing, moving, and shaking, and from reciprocal causes and conditions; if it arises from reciprocal conditions, it cannot reveal the first principle. The first principle has no marks of self or other, and speech, having marks, cannot reveal it. The first principle is only one's own mind; all manner of external thoughts are entirely nonexistent, and verbal discrimination cannot reveal it. Therefore, Mahāmati, one should keep far from verbal discrimination.”
“All dharmas have no self-nature, and likewise there is no speaking of them;
Not seeing the meaning of emptiness as emptiness, the foolish therefore wander on.
All dharmas have no nature, beyond words and discrimination;
All existences are like a dream and an illusion, neither birth and death nor nirvāṇa.
As a king or an elder, to make his children rejoice,
First shows them things that resemble the real, and afterward gives them what is true.
So too do I: first I teach a dharma that resembles the real;
And afterward I unfold for them the dharma of self-realized reality.”

Then Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, I pray you teach me of being free from oneness and difference, from both and neither, from being and non-being, from neither being nor non-being, and from permanence and impermanence—the realm of self-realized holy wisdom, which all the sectarians cannot practice, free of the vain clinging to self-marks and common marks, entering the true realm of the first principle, gradually purifying the grounds and entering the Tathāgata's rank, and by the power of effortless original vows, like a wish-fulfilling jewel, universally manifesting all boundless realms. May all dharmas be seen as the distinctions of one's own mind, so that I and the other Bodhisattvas, regarding such dharmas as these, may depart from the views of the imagined self-nature and its self-marks and common marks, swiftly realize anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, and cause all beings to be complete and perfect in all merits.”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, excellent, excellent! Out of compassion for the world you ask me this meaning; it is of great benefit and great peace. Mahāmati, ordinary people, lacking wisdom, do not know the measure of the mind; with vain habit as their cause they cling to external things and discriminate all the self-natures of oneness and difference, both and neither, being and non-being, neither being nor non-being, permanence and impermanence. Mahāmati, as a herd of beasts, tormented by thirst, gives rise to the thought of water in a hot mirage, and confusedly runs toward it, not knowing it is not water—so too is the foolish ordinary person: perfumed by beginningless idle talk and discrimination, with the three poisons burning his mind, he delights in realms of form, sees arising, abiding, and ceasing, grasps inner and outer dharmas, and falls into the clinging to oneness and difference and the rest. Mahāmati, as a city of the gandharvas is neither a city nor not a city, and yet the unwise, from beginningless time, because of the habit-energy of clinging to the notion of a city, form the thought of a city—so too the sectarians, perfumed by beginningless false habits, cannot comprehend what appears in their own mind, and cling to the various words of oneness and difference and the rest. Mahāmati, as a person in a dream sees men and women, elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers, cities, towns, gardens, and all manner of adornments, and upon waking remembers those unreal things—Mahāmati, what do you think? Is such a person wise?”
He answered: “No.”

“Mahāmati, so too the sectarians: devoured by evil views, they do not comprehend mind-only, and cling to views of oneness and difference, being and non-being, and the rest. Mahāmati, as a painted image has neither height nor depth, yet the foolish falsely see it and form thoughts of height and depth—so too will the sectarians of the future be: their evil views and habits grow, their false minds increase, and clinging to oneness and difference and the rest, they ruin themselves and ruin others. Toward the teaching of freedom from being and non-being and of non-arising, they say it is nonexistent; this slanders cause and effect and uproots the roots of goodness. One should know that such a person, discriminating being and non-being, gives rise to views of self and other, and will fall into the hells; one who wishes to seek the supreme dharma should swiftly keep far from them. Mahāmati, as one with a diseased eye sees a hair-net, and people say to one another that this is rare; and yet this hair-net is neither existent nor nonexistent, because it is seen and not seen—so too the sectarians: with evil views they discriminate and cling to oneness and difference, both and neither, and the rest, slandering the true Dharma and drowning themselves and others. Mahāmati, as a fire-wheel is in truth no wheel, yet the foolish grasp at it, though not the wise—so too the sectarians: with evil views and desires they cling to oneness and difference, both and neither, and the rest, as the arising of all dharmas. Mahāmati, as a water-bubble resembles a crystal bead, and the foolish, taking it as real, run to seize it; and yet that water-bubble is neither a bead nor not a bead, because it is grasped and not grasped—so too the sectarians, perfumed by the habit-energy of evil discrimination, speak of what is not compounded as arising and so destroy dependent existence.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, having established the three measures, they give rise to the discrimination of a nature regarding the dharma of the holy wisdom of inner realization, which is free of the two self-natures. Mahāmati, the cultivators who turn mind, manas, and consciousness, and are free of the grasped and the grasping, abide in the Tathāgata's ground of self-realized holy dharma, and give rise to no thought of being or non-being. Mahāmati, if cultivators give rise to the clinging to being and non-being regarding realms, they cling to self, person, being, and life. Mahāmati, the self-marks and common marks of all dharmas are taught by the Manifestation Buddha, not by the Dharma Buddha. Mahāmati, what the Manifestation Buddha teaches accords only with the views that arise in the foolish; it is not for the revealing of the blissful realm of the samādhi of self-realized holy wisdom. Mahāmati, as the image of a tree appears in water—it is neither an image nor not an image, neither a tree's shape nor not a tree's shape. So too the sectarians, perfumed by their views, do not comprehend their own mind, and give rise to discrimination regarding oneness and difference and the rest. Mahāmati, as a bright mirror has no discrimination, and yet shows all forms and colors in accord with the various conditions—it is neither an image nor not an image, and one sees the image as no image, yet the foolish discriminate and form the thought of an image. So too the sectarians, regarding the various forms and images that appear in their own mind, cling to the marks of oneness and difference, both and neither. Mahāmati, as an echo in a valley arises from the conjunction of the sounds of wind, water, and people—it is neither existent nor nonexistent, because the sound heard is no sound. So too the sectarians, by the power of the habit-energy of their own mental discrimination, give rise to views of oneness and difference, both and neither. Mahāmati, as on a great earth devoid of grass and trees, touched by the sunlight, flame-like water waves move—they are neither existent nor nonexistent, because an inverted thought is no thought. So too the foolish ordinary person, perfumed by beginningless idle talk and evil habits, within the gate of the dharma-nature of holy wisdom and self-realization sees the natures of arising, abiding, and ceasing, of oneness and difference, of being and non-being, of both and neither. Mahāmati, as a wooden man or a reanimated corpse, by the power of a piśāca or a mechanism, moves and turns and acts without cease, and the unwise take it as real—so too the foolish ordinary person, following the sectarians, gives rise to all evil views and clings to the false words of oneness and difference and the rest. Therefore, Mahāmati, within the dharma realized by holy wisdom, you should be free of all discrimination of arising, abiding, and ceasing, of oneness and difference, of being and non-being, of both and neither, and the rest.”
“The five aggregates of the consciousnesses are like the image of a tree in water;
What is seen is like an illusion and a dream; one should not vainly discriminate.
The three realms are like a mirage, an illusion, a dream, and a hair-net;
If one can observe thus, one attains ultimate liberation.
As a mirage in the heat moves and confuses the mind;
The thirsty beast takes it for water, though in truth there is no water there.
So too does the seed of consciousness move and see realms;
As what the diseased eye sees, so the foolish give rise to clinging.
In beginningless birth and death, covered by the clinging to objects;
One turns away and forsakes them, causing one to go forth, like a snare set for a hare.
Made by illusion, spell, and mechanism, a floating cloud, a dream, a flash of lightning;
Observing the world as ever thus, one forever cuts off the three continuities.
Herein there is nothing whatsoever, like a mirage in the sky;
Knowing all dharmas thus, one then knows nothing at all.
The aggregates are like a hair-net; within them one vainly discriminates;
It is only a name falsely set up; the marks sought are unobtainable.
Like a painted image, hanging hair, an illusion, a dream, a gandharva city;
A fire-wheel, a hot mirage—in truth nonexistent, yet seen as existent.
Thus permanence and impermanence, oneness and difference, both and neither;
Because of beginningless bondage, the foolish vainly discriminate.
A bright mirror, clear water, and a pure eye, a wonderful maṇi jewel;
